key_insight: Short motion-sensor recordings during hair combing and toothbrushing showed promise for distinguishing Parkinson’s disease and identifying patient-reported functional impairment.
clinical_relevance: Sensor-equipped everyday tools could complement clinical assessments with quantitative measures of task-specific functional ability.
method: Collected inertial measurement unit data from toothbrushes and hair combs during daily-living tasks.
Split signals into non-overlapping 3–9-second intervals and extracted 30 motion features per interval.
Trained XGBoost classifiers to assess disease status, severity, symptoms, and functional impairment.
evidence_signal: In a pilot study of 39 people with Parkinson’s disease and 7 healthy controls, hair-combing models achieved balanced accuracies of 0.864 for disease status and 0.869 for patient-reported functional impairment; toothbrushing models achieved 0.752 and 0.686, respectively.
watch_item: The small pilot cohort, particularly the seven controls, limits generalizability; larger independent validation is needed before clinical implementation.
paper_title: Short intervals of inertial measurement unit data collected during activities of daily living can provide a quantitative method to assess disease severity and functional ability in Parkinson's disease
